title: Raga Ramkali
hookLine: a calm morning raga, home of Guru Nanak's talks with the yogis, that opens by setting learning aside for the one Name

cards: Some read Sanskrit. Some read the old Puranas. Some sit with a string of beads, counting the Name, fixed in meditation.

That's how today's raga begins, on ang eight seventy-six of the Guru Granth Sahib: a quick tour of serious religious people doing serious religious things. A listener might expect the next line to pick a winner.
It doesn't. Guru Nanak steps out of the lineup altogether, and what he says next is very quiet. Today: Raga Ramkali.

teach.b: Ramkali follows Gond in the Granth's order, and Sikh tradition hears it as a calm morning raga.

teach.h: I RECOGNIZE ONLY YOUR ONE NAME.
teach.b: First, the opening hymn's turn, in paraphrase: I know nothing, now or ever; I recognize only your one Name. Then the refrain: I don't know, Lord, what my state is.
And: I'm foolish and without understanding; I've come to your shelter; be kind, and keep my honor. No reader is mocked, no bead-counter is scorned. Guru Nanak simply doesn't compete.
Where others show what they know, he admits what he doesn't, and rests in the Name. That's the calm. Second, the yogis.

Ramkali is where the Granth holds Guru Nanak's talks with the yogis, the wandering ascetics with their earrings, horns and begging bags; tomorrow brings the Sidh Gosht, his long conversation with them.

In another Ramkali hymn, Guru Nanak takes up their own gear, in paraphrase: awareness of the Word is my horn, and the world hears it sound; honor is my begging bag, and the Name is the alms I receive.
Tradition says the yogis honored a master called Gorakh. The hymn's refrain answers: the true Gorakh is the One who lifted up the earth and made it without delay. Third, together.
In Ramkali the outward signs of religion, scholarship, beads, earrings, horns, are each turned inward and pointed at the Name. Nothing is thrown away; everything goes deeper.

how: Shabads from the Ramkali section of the Guru Granth Sahib are sung in kirtan in Raga Ramkali, which Sikh musical tradition associates with a calm morning mood.

o: a raga of wedding songs and the four Lavan rounds
the calm morning raga after Gond, home of the yogi talks
an evening raga sung only by wandering yogis

games.q: inside raga Ramkali — tap the pairs.
p: the One who lifted up the earth

s: Ramkali's opening hymn mocks scholars and bead-counters
it names them without scorn, and Nanak simply rests in the one Name.
Ramkali holds Guru Nanak's talks with the yogis
the Granth sets his conversations with the yogis in Ramkali.
in Ramkali, Guru Nanak tells the yogis to throw away their horns
he turns the horn inward: awareness of the Word is my horn.

games.q: a lineup of the devout: one reads Sanskrit, one reads the Puranas, one counts beads. it's your turn. what do you say?
o: say you know nothing, and recognize only the one Name.
explain why the others are doing it wrong.
games.why: Guru Nanak says: I know nothing, now or ever; I recognize only your one Name. he doesn't compete, and he doesn't scorn.

practice: Let the breath slow until it's barely noticeable, then for two minutes set down whatever you know, what you've read, what you believe, what you'd argue for, not thrown away, just placed beside you.
Sit with one word, or with nothing, the way a still lake sits under the morning, letting Waheguru be that word if you pray.

wordCard.voice: Raga Ramkali. The calm morning raga after Gond, home of Guru Nanak's talks with the yogis, which opens with I recognize only your one Name. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: calm and deep. The Word is the horn the world hears. Rest well.
